rows.description: A child who has moved schools remembers the old class as perfect and forgets the quarrels. Distance smooths rough edges of the past.
A teenager feeling pressure remembers early childhood as carefree and longs for it, forgetting its fears and limits. Comfort and loss colour the picture.
A student in a hostel far from home idealises home life and old friends, and may feel homesick with love mixed with a bit of avoidance of present challenges.
A toddler opens every drawer, tastes leaves and pulls things apart. Curiosity is the engine of early learning, and safety-proofing works better than constant saying no.
A child asks why the sky is blue, why grandma is old, why the moon follows the car. Answers matter less than an adult who treats the questions as worth answering.
A teenager explores sex, religion, risky videos or rebellious ideas partly from real interest. Curiosity that is met with panic goes underground, while calm answers keep the door open.

A hearing or deaf toddler may use signs or gestures for "more", "milk" or "all done" before speech. Deaf children exposed to a signed language from birth learn it on the same timetable as spoken languages.
A school-age signer fingerspells names or unfamiliar words and uses name signs given by the community. Fingerspelling is a tool within a full language, not the language itself.

rows.subtype: Sign language in workplaces and public life [Expressing]
rows.description: A young signer works through interpreters or video relay and expects equal access. Colleagues can learn a few signs, face the person and avoid assumptions about ability.

rows.subtype: Hitting a sibling after being scolded [Actor]
rows.description: A toddler told off by a parent turns and pushes a younger sibling or throws a toy; the anger has no safe target so it lands on someone smaller and less threatening.

rows.subtype: Kicking the bag after a teacher's rebuke [Actor]
rows.description: A child humiliated in class comes home and slams doors or snaps at the family dog; the feeling belongs to school but is spent where it feels safe.
A child is told by an older student or adult to hide something, pick on someone or keep a secret. They feel a pull between obedience and a stomach-sinking sense of wrongness.

rows.subtype: Teacher or coach crossing a line [Receiver]
rows.description: A student is pressured by a coach, tutor or senior to do something that feels wrong, with respect and fear mixed. They may freeze or comply because refusing an authority feels unthinkable.
A toddler believes that his wish or a gesture can make things happen, such as a wave making a toy move. He cannot yet separate thought from the physical world.
A preschooler believes in monsters under the bed, the tooth fairy and special words that protect him. Imagination is vivid and the line with reality is soft.
An older child avoids stepping on cracks, taps things or wears a lucky shirt for exams. He half knows it is not logical and still feels safer with it.
